target_claim:
All graphs are finite, undirected, and simple. A graph is triangle-free if it has no three distinct pairwise adjacent vertices. Let G have vertex set V(G)={v_1,...,v_n}, where n=|V(G)|>=2, and suppose G is triangle-free. Write deg_G(v_i) for the degree of v_i, and let 0 be a symbol distinct from 1,...,n. Construct H with
V(H)={{i,j}: i,j in {1,...,n}, v_i v_j in E(G), and deg_G(v_i)>1} union {{0,i}: i in {1,...,n} and deg_G(v_i)=1},
where two distinct vertices p,q of H are adjacent exactly when p intersect q is nonempty.

Let K_4^- denote the graph on four vertices with five edges. For a K_4^--free graph X and e,e' in E(X), define e~e' when the endpoints of e and e' together span a clique in X. This is an equivalence relation. For e in E(X), let C_X(e) be the clique consisting of all endpoints of edges in the equivalence class of e. Define B(X) to be the graph whose vertices are the distinct cliques C_X(e), e in E(X), with two distinct such cliques adjacent exactly when their intersection is nonempty.

For each i in {1,...,n}, put C_i={p in V(H): i in p}. The claim is that H is K_4^--free; every C_i is one of the vertices C_H(e) of B(H); the C_i are pairwise distinct and exhaust V(B(H)); and the map phi:V(G)->V(B(H)) given by phi(v_i)=C_i is a graph isomorphism. Equivalently, in addition to being a bijection, it satisfies v_i v_j in E(G) if and only if C_i and C_j are adjacent in B(H), for every distinct i,j.
source_quote:
In this document, $\tf$ denotes the family of all triangle-free graphs, and $\ltf$ is the family of all graphs $G$ such that $G$ is the line graph of some $H\in\tf$. We denote the line graph of $G$ by $G^*$. We use $R$ to denote a graph relation, with superscripts ($R^G$, $R^{G'}$) when necessary; edges are often denoted by their endpoints as $vv'$. Throughout, $R^G(v)=\{w\in G: R^G(v,w)\}$, with the superscripts dropped whenever possible.

We call any graph isomorphic to $\kit$ a \emph{claw}, and we refer to the graph on four vertices with five edges as $\kk$.

Let $G=(V(G),E(G))$ be a $\kk$-free graph. Then the relation $\sim$ on $E(G)$ given by $e\sim e'$ if the endpoints of $e,e'$ span a clique in $G$ is an equivalence relation. The $\sim$ classes are cliques, and two distinct classes are either disjoint or have exactly one vertex in common.

It is clear from the definition of $\sim$ that for any $e$, $\cup e/\sim$ is a clique in $G$.

If $G$ is a $\kk$-free graph and $e=xy$ is an edge in $G$, we use $\cls e$ or $\cls{xy}$ to denote the $\sim$-class of $e$.

Let $G$ be a $\kk$-free graph, and $e\in E(G)$. The \emph{block graph} $B(G)$ of $G$ is the graph $$(\{\cls e:e\in E(G)\}, \{(\cls e,\cls{e'}):\cls e\cap \cls{e'}\neq\varnothing\}).$$

Every finite triangle-free graph $G$ is $B(H)$ for some $H\in\ltf$.

It sufficess to show the proposition for connected graphs, as the same argument can be carried out in each connected component of a disconnected graph. If $G$ consists of a single vertex, then $G$ is the block graph of any clique, corresponding to the block graph of the line graph of a star. We assume now that $G$ contains at least two vertices.

Given a triangle-free graph $G$ with vertex set $\{v_1,\ldots,v_n\}$, we need to find a $\kk-,\kit$-free graph $H$ with $B(H)\cong G$. Let $H$ be the graph with vertex set $\{\{i,j\}:G\models R(v_i,v_j), \deg(v_i)>1\}\cup\{\{0,i\}:\deg(v_i)=1\}$, where the graph relation holds if $\{i,j\}\cap\{k,l\}\neq\varnothing$.

The graph $H$ is an induced subgraph of the line graph of the complete graph on $\{1,\ldots n\}$, and thus a line graph, so in particular $\kit$-free. A $\kk$ can only be obtained from vertices of degree at least two in $G$, so we would have vertices $\{i,j\},\{i,l\},\{i,m\}\{l,m\}$ in $H$. But this means that the triangle $i,l,m$ appears in $G$, contradicting triangle-freeness. Therefore $H$ is the line graph of some triangle-free graph.

The blocks of $H$ are maximal sets of pairs with nonempty intersection. If we denote the maximal clique in $H$ with intersection $\{m\}$ by $C_m$ , then
the function $v_i\mapsto C_i$ is an isomorphism between $B(H)$ and $G$.
The block graph of $H$ is isomorphic to $G$.
